title: What Part 1 Is and Why It Matters
blocks: Part 1 is the first 4-5 minutes of the test. After checking your identity, the examiner chooses three topics — the first is almost always about your **work/study** or your **hometown/home**, and the other two can be any everyday subject (food, weather, sport, music, technology, etc.). Each topic has 3-4 short questions. The questions are **about you** — your habits, likes and experiences. There are no abstract or social questions here; those come in Part 3.
Many people take Part 1 lightly — "they're easy questions, I'll just say something". That's a mistake. Part 1 matters for three reasons:
**First impression.** The examiner forms an idea of you in the first two minutes. To change that idea later, you have to do a lot better.

**There are no excuses here.** If you get stuck on a difficult question in Part 3, the examiner understands that the topic is hard. But if you get stuck on "What do you do in your free time?", they assume you don't have basic fluency.
**This is your warm-up.** If Part 1 goes well, you go into Part 2 relaxed. If it goes badly, your nervousness grows and stays with you for the whole test.
How long should an answer be?

The most practical rule for Part 1: **2 to 4 sentences**. If you answer in one word or one sentence, you aren't giving the examiner a chance to hear your language. On the other hand, if you speak for 1 minute on a single Part 1 question, the examiner will stop you — and they will have less time to ask the next questions in their script. Answer + reason + one detail — that's the right size.

✗ **Q:** Do you often use public transport?
**Too short:** Yes, every day.

✗ **Too long:** Yes, I use public transport every day. I take the bus in the morning at 8 o'clock. The bus is number 27. It goes from my area to Motijheel. It takes one hour. Sometimes it takes one and a half hours. There is a lot of traffic. I don't like the traffic. Many people are on the bus. Sometimes I have to stand. When I stand it is difficult. After that I reach my office...
Long, but all simple sentences with no linking, and the examiner will stop you after 30 seconds.
**The right size:** Yes, pretty much every day, actually. I take the bus to work since it's by far the cheapest option, although the traffic on my route can be a nightmare during rush hour.
Every Part 1 question fits one of three patterns. If you can recognise the pattern as soon as you hear the question, your answer organises itself.

**Strategy 1 — Direct Answer + Extension (2 steps)**
**When:** simple, factual questions — your name, your work, your home, how long, who you live with. No reason is asked for here; one extra piece of information is enough.

**Step 1 — Direct Answer:** answer directly, in one sentence.

**Step 2 — Extension:** one related detail — how long, with whom, what it's like, what it involves.
**Q:** Where do you live?
**Direct Answer:** I live in a rented flat in the eastern part of the city, **Extension:** about ten minutes' walk from my office, which is the main reason we chose it.
**Q:** Do you work or study?
**Direct Answer:** I'm working at the moment — I'm a pharmacist at a hospital. **Extension:** I've been there just over three years now, mostly on the night shift.

**Strategy 2 — A.R.E: Answer – Reason – Example (3 steps)**
**When:** questions with a hidden "why" — Do you like...? Do you prefer...? Is ... important? Would you like to...? Most Part 1 questions follow this pattern.

**Step 1 — Answer:** a clear yes/no/it depends.

**Step 2 — Reason:** because / since / mainly because / the thing is.

**Step 3 — Example:** a concrete example or situation from your own life.
**Q:** Do you prefer tea or coffee?
**Answer:** Tea, without a doubt. **Reason:** Partly it's habit — I grew up in a house where the kettle was always on — but I also find coffee makes me jittery. **Example:** Last month I switched to coffee for a week to stay awake for exams and barely slept, so I went straight back to tea.
**Q:** Is it important to have a good relationship with your neighbours?
**Answer:** I think so, yes, especially in a city. **Reason:** Your family might be hundreds of kilometres away, and your neighbours are the only people close enough to help in an emergency. **Example:** When our electricity went out for a whole night last summer, the family upstairs lent us a lamp and kept our food in their fridge.

**Strategy 3 — L.D.F: Likes – Frequency – Reason (3 steps)**
**When:** questions about hobbies, free time, routines and habits — What do you do in your free time? Do you play any sport? How often do you...? With these questions, the listener wants to know both "what you do" and "how often".

**Step 1 — Likes:** what you like doing (use different verbs: I'm into, I'm keen on, I spend a lot of time...).

**Step 2 — Frequency:** how often and when (from the frequency list above).

**Step 3 — Reason:** why you enjoy it / what it gives you.
**Q:** What do you like doing at the weekend?
**Likes:** I'm quite into cycling these days. **Frequency:** I try to go out every Friday morning, usually for an hour or so before the roads get busy. **Reason:** It's the only time in the week when I'm not looking at a screen, and I come back with a much clearer head.
**Q:** Do you listen to music?
**Likes:** All the time — mostly old Bangla band songs, and some instrumental stuff when I'm working. **Frequency:** Pretty much daily; my commute alone is an hour of music. **Reason:** On a crowded bus it's the one thing that makes the journey bearable, and it puts me in a decent mood before I reach the office.

**Which one when — at a glance:** The question doesn't ask for a reason (what/where/how long) → **Direct Answer + Extension**. The question involves a preference, an opinion or a "why" → **A.R.E**. The question is about habits or free time → **L.D.F**. If in doubt, use A.R.E — it works everywhere.
If we break the three strategies down a little further, Part 1 questions fall into **7 types**. Next to each one is the strategy that works best for it.
Do you like...? / Are you interested in...? / Is ... important to you?
Clear yes/no (or "it depends") → reason → one detail. "Not really, to be honest. I find ... a bit ..., so I'd rather ..."
How often do you...? / Do you often...?
Frequency phrase → when/in what situation → why. "Maybe two or three times a month, usually at weekends when..."
Do you prefer A or B? / Which do you like more?
Preference → reason → exception. "I'd go for A most of the time, mainly because ... Having said that, when ..., B works better."
What's your ... like? / Tell me about ... / What kind of ... do you...?
General picture → 2 specific details → your feelings. "It's a fairly ... place. There's ... and ..., and I quite like the fact that ..."
Did you ... when you were a child? / Has ... changed?
Past (used to / past simple) → now (present) → reason/feeling. "When I was a kid I used to ..., but these days I ... , mostly because ..."
Would you like to ... in the future? / Will you ...?
Wish → condition → reason. "I'd love to, if I ever get the chance, because ..."
Do you think ... is important? / Why do people...?
Opinion → reason → your own example. "I think so, yes. It ..., and in my own case ..."
**Answer in the first sentence.** "Do you like cooking?" → your first word should be Yes/No/Sort of/It depends — no introduction.
**Don't hand the question's words back.** "Do you like cooking?" → "Yes, I like cooking" (weak) vs "Yes, I'm quite into it, actually" (good).
**Never stop at Yes/No.** Always add "because", "since", "the thing is".
**Keep your present tense accurate.** Most Part 1 questions are about habits — "I go", "she works", "it takes". Don't forget the third-person -s.
**Use degree adverbs instead of 'very':** quite, pretty, fairly, really, absolutely, a bit, not particularly.
**Give one concrete detail.** Compared with "I like music", "I like music — mostly old Bangla band songs from the nineties" gives the examiner far more language.
**Give the answer that gives you more to say.** Nobody checks whether it's true.
**One or two Part 3-style questions may come up** ("Why do you think people like ...?"). Don't panic; give a brief opinion, give a reason, and move on.
"How often" questions are very common in Part 1. Don't use only "sometimes" and "always" — add variety from the list below.
pretty much every day, almost daily, as a rule, without fail, whenever I get the chance
a couple of times a week, every other day, most weekends, fairly regularly, on a regular basis
now and then, from time to time, every so often, once in a while, occasionally
hardly ever, rarely, once in a blue moon, not as often as I'd like, only on special occasions
never, not at all, I've never actually..., it's just not something I do

Now for the topic bank. For each topic, ★★★ next to a question means it is very common in the test, ★★ means it comes up sometimes, and ★ means it comes up less often — but this categorisation is based on my own experience; any of them can come up in the test. After reading each model answer, **put in your own information** and say your own answer out loud — that's the practice.

title: How to Build Your Own Answers for Part 1
blocks: Reading the 130 answers above doesn't mean you're ready for Part 1. Apply the method below to all 32 topics — about 8-10 hours of work in total, and after that no Part 1 question will take you by surprise.

**Write down 3 true facts about yourself for each topic.** Work: where, how long, the best/worst thing about it. Food: your favourite food, whether you can cook, what you don't eat. These are your "raw material".
**Choose a precise word or collocation for each fact.** Not "I like my job" — but "I find it rewarding / it's fairly demanding / the hours are flexible".
**Using the 7 question patterns (above), say 3 answers out loud for each topic**, record them and listen back.
**Listen to the recording and look for three things:** where you say "umm", which words keep coming up, and which answers end after a single word. These are the areas to work on.

**A week later, speak on the same topic again — without looking.** If the main ideas come back but the words are a little different, you're on the right track. If exactly the same sentences come out, you've memorised them — and the examiner will notice.

**Final word:** The best Part 1 answer is one that sounds as if you're chatting with a friend at a tea stall — just in English, and a little more organised. The examiner doesn't want anything more than that.
